newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's PDI may lose its place in parliament.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's PDI may lose its place in parliament.

text.p: The fragmented minority Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), whose share of the vote plummeted in last week's general election, said on Tuesday it might have to withdraw from parliament.
"We may have to quit the House (of Representatives) if we fail to make the minimum representation," PDI deputy chairman Harsoko Sudiro told Reuters.

Under parliament's current rules, each of the three legal parties must have at least one representative assigned uniquely to each of the 11 commissions which carry out the bulk of the work in the 500-seat assembly.

The PDI, badly split over a leadership battle, had only 10 seats after last Thursday's poll, down from 56 won in the last election in 1992. Its share of the vote plunged to three percent from 15 percent in the previous poll.

The ruling Golkar, assured of victory even before the ballot, exceeded its official expectations with a sweeping 74 percent of the vote, while its main rival, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) took 22.7 percent.
The House of Representatives has 425 elected seats, with the other 75 filled by the military which does not vote in the general elections.
Political analysts said President Suharto, in power for the last 30 years, had based the country's politics on a three-party system created in the early 1970s.
Mohammad Hikam, a political scientist at the Indonesian Academy of Sciences, said he believed the government would intervene to prevent a PDI withdrawal.
"I don't think the government will allow such thing to happen because it will give a bad precedent. Or maybe the House will have to change its internal regulations if the PDI does quit," he said.
The PDI fragmented after a government-backed faction ousted Megawati Sukarnoputri, popular eldest daughter of Indonesia's late founding president Sukarno, as PDI leader last year.
Megawati herself refused to vote last Thursday, and advised her supporters not to cast their ballots for the government-recognised wing of the PDI headed by deputy parliamentary speaker Surjadi.
Megawati, a member of the previous legislature, and her supporters were barred by the election commission from running this year.
PDI deputy chairman Harsoko said the party was still discussing what to do. It appeared likely that Surjadi himself, who ran in Jakarta, would also lose his seat for lack of votes.
Vote counting is still going on and the election's final results will be announced on June 17.
Hikam said he believed Megawati's decision not to vote and her plea to her supporters played "a big role in the drop in the PDI's share".
The PPP has alleged widespread irregularities in the poll, but Hikam said if the PDI blamed election fraud for its disastrous showing this would only be an excuse.
Political analysts said the PDI's official leader Surjadi had lost credibility before the poll after being seen to be a tool of the government.

Analysts said the government had ousted Megawati for fear of her vote drawing potential, and also for fear that she might pose a challenge to Suharto, who is widely expected to run for a seventh five-year term in office next March.
